Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Energy Corp Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] Please note this event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to John Smith, VP of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

John Smith: Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Apex Energy Corp's Q3 2024 earnings call. Joining me on the call today are David Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; Sarah Jenkins, Chief Financial Officer; Michael Rodriguez, Chief Operating Officer; and Lisa Chen, VP of Exploration.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we make today may be forward-looking. These statements are based on current expectations and assumptions and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of these risks.

I will now turn the call over to David Thompson.

David Thompson: Thank you, John, and good morning, everyone. Apex Energy Corp delivered solid results in Q3, driven by strong operational performance and favorable commodity prices. We achieved robust production growth averaging 285,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, with meaningful quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year increases in both oil and gas volumes. I'm particularly pleased with our progress on proved reserves additions, boasting a reserve replacement ratio well above 400% and strong organic growth from the drillbit across our key basins. We maintained disciplined capital allocation reflected in our debt reduction, with total debt down significantly and leverage ratios at the low end of our targets. Further, our refining segment posted record throughput and resilient margins amid crack spread strength. Finally, we are taking steps to advance our ESG initiatives, making substantial headway on emissions reduction targets that enhance our long-term sustainability.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Sarah Jenkins to discuss our financial results in more detail.

Sarah Jenkins: Thank you, David. As David mentioned, we had a strong quarter. Our revenue was $5.8 billion, up 25% year-over-year. Operating income was $2.1 billion, and net income was $1.4 billion. We generated $1.8 billion in free cash flow and returned $1.1 billion to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases. Our balance sheet remains strong, with $12.4 billion in total debt, $9.8 billion in net debt, and leverage at 1.2x net debt to LTM Adjusted EBITDA. We ended with $2.6 billion in cash.

Good afternoon, everyone. As we review our balance sheet strength, I'd like to dive deep into our debt profile, which continues to reflect disciplined capital allocation and robust free cash flow generation amid a constructive macro environment. With Brent averaging $82 per barrel in Q3 and WTI at $77, supported by ongoing OPEC+ production discipline and resilient global demand, we've leveraged our high-margin assets to meaningfully deleverage. Let me walk you through the key metrics: total debt, net debt, and our leverage ratios, with some color on trends, initiatives, and forward strategy.

Total debt stood at $12.4 billion at quarter-end, down 8% or $1.1 billion from year-end 2023. This reduction was driven primarily by $850 million in principal repayments on our term loan B facilities, funded through excess free cash flow from our Permian Basin operations, where our Tier 1 acreage delivered over 60% EBITDA margins. Short-term debt, including our $500 million commercial paper program, remains minimal at just $200 million, providing flexibility without straining liquidity. Long-term debt comprises 92% of the total, with a weighted average maturity of 4.8 years and a blended coupon of 4.2%—a testament to our proactive refinancing last year. Notably, we extended $3 billion of our 2026 maturities into 2029 and 2031 tranches at sub-4% yields, locking in savings of approximately 150 basis points versus pre-2022 rates. This positions us favorably against peers like Pioneer Natural Resources or Occidental, who have faced higher refinancing costs on legacy debt.

Moving to net debt, which we define as total debt minus cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments, we ended Q3 at $9.8 billion—a 12% year-over-year decline and our lowest level since pre-COVID. This reflects $2.6 billion in cash on hand, bolstered by $1.2 billion in restricted cash tied to our Gulf of Mexico JV with Shell on the Vito project. The sequential $400 million reduction came from strong operating cash flow of $2.1 billion in the quarter, exceeding capex by $1.4 billion, allowing us to prepay debt without dipping into our $4 billion undrawn revolving credit facility—RCF utilization sits at a pristine 15%. Regionally, our Bakken assets contributed disproportionately, with net debt there falling 20% YoY on the back of 15% production growth to 120,000 boe/d, fueled by long laterals and enhanced completions averaging 4,500 lateral feet with 60-stage fracs.

Now, turning to leverage ratios, our headline metric—net debt to LTM Adjusted EBITDA—improved to 1.2x from 1.6x at year-end 2023 and 2.1x at the pandemic trough. This places us at the lower end of our mid-cycle target range of 0.8x to 1.5x, ahead of industry medians per S&P Global data, where supermajors like Chevron hover around 1.0x and independents like EOG Resources at 0.5x. For context, LTM EBITDA hit $8.2 billion, up 15% YoY, driven by realized pricing of $68/boe and opex control at $9.50/boe. Our debt-to-EBITDA covenant under the RCF remains comfortably at 2.8x headroom versus 3.5x limits, with interest coverage at 12x EBITDA/interest. We've also maintained an investment-grade profile, with ratings affirmed at BBB-/Baa3 from S&P and Moody's, reflecting our 65% fixed-rate debt mix and minimal exposure to floating rates amid Fed rate cuts.

Strategically, this deleveraging supports our capital return framework: we returned $1.1 billion to shareholders in Q3 via $600 million in base dividends (yield now 3.2%) and $500 million in buybacks under our $3 billion authorization. Looking ahead, we expect net debt to dip below $9 billion by year-end 2024, assuming $75-85 Brent, as we generate $6-7 billion in free cash flow on $5.5 billion capex—skewed 70% to Permian development drilling and 20% to high-return Guyana pre-FID investments alongside ExxonMobil. Technical initiatives include a $500 million asset monetization in the Rockies, targeted for close in Q4, and hedging 55% of 2025 oil volumes at $75 WTI floors to buffer volatility from Red Sea disruptions or potential China demand softness.

Regionally, Permian leverage is sub-0.5x standalone, thanks to D&C efficiencies yielding 10% IRR hurdles at $60 oil; Bakken at 1.0x with NGL uplift from Montney takeaway expansions; and offshore GoM at 1.8x, where we're accelerating Thunder Horse South tie-backs for 20,000 boe/d incremental by 2026. Internationally, our North Sea portfolio remains self-funding at 0.9x leverage post-Brexit fiscal stability.

In summary, our debt levels underscore Apex's fortress balance sheet: total debt down 8%, net debt down 12%, leverage at 1.2x, with ample liquidity for growth, returns, and resilience in a $70-90 oil world. We're not just managing debt—we're optimizing it to create long-term value.

I'd also like to touch on our proved reserves additions, reserve replacement ratio—or RRR—and the robust organic growth that's underpinning our long-term value creation. As you know, in the upstream Oil & Gas sector, reserves are the lifeblood of our business, and we've delivered exceptional results here that position us for decades of low-cost inventory.

At year-end 2023, our total proved reserves stood at 2.8 billion barrels of oil equivalent—or BOE—up 12% from 2.5 billion BOE at the end of 2022. This reflects total additions of 520 million BOE during the year. To put that in context, our 2023 production was 112 million BOE, a 5% increase year-over-year driven by our Permian and Eagle Ford programs.

Our total reserve replacement ratio came in at an outstanding 465%, calculated as (positive revisions + extensions + discoveries + acquisitions - divestitures) divided by annual production. Breaking it down: extensions and discoveries added 320 million BOE, primarily from successful delineation and development drilling; revisions contributed a positive 85 million BOE, thanks to better-than-expected well performance and lower decline curves in our core basins; acquisitions brought in 140 million BOE, including our bolt-on acquisition of 50,000 net acres in the Delaware Basin from a private seller—high-quality Tier 1 acreage with stacked pay zones analogous to Pioneer's pre-Exxon merger assets; divestitures were minimal at 25 million BOE, non-core shallow gas assets in the Mid-Continent that we monetized at a 4x multiple to free up capital.

Even more impressive is our organic reserve replacement ratio, excluding M&A, which clocked in at 380%. This is organic growth at its finest—purely from the drillbit—and marks our sixth straight year above 200%. Over the past five years, our organic RRR averages 285%, well above the industry's long-term benchmark of 100% for sustainability, and competitive with peers like EOG Resources or Diamondback Energy, who've posted similar multi-year figures in the Permian.

Regionally, our portfolio diversification is a key strategic edge. Permian Basin, 65% of reserves, saw 280 million BOE added organically. We booked 150 million BOE from extensions in the Delaware sub-basin, leveraging our proprietary full-waveform inversion seismic data to high-grade Wolfcamp A and Bone Springs intervals. Our average lateral length hit 12,500 feet this year, with proppant intensity up 15% to 2,500 pounds per foot, driving initial production rates of 1,800 BOE/d per well—10% above type curve. Breakevens here are sub-$35 WTI, insulating us from volatility.

Eagle Ford, 20% of reserves, added 120 million BOE in organic additions, fueled by our Pearsall Shale pilot program. We've converted 40% of our proved undeveloped—or PUD—locations to proved developed producing, or PDP, through hydraulic fracturing optimizations like diverter technology and engineered completions. This reversed prior negative revisions and positions us for 10% production growth in 2024.

Bakken and DJ Basin, 10% of reserves, added 65 million BOE, with standout discoveries in the Three Forks benchmark interval. Our extended laterals—up to 15,000 feet—are yielding 1,200 BOE/d IPs, and we're applying machine learning for fracture design to boost EURs by 20%.

International and offshore, 5% of reserves, contributed 55 million BOE from Gulf of Mexico extensions and a farm-in deal offshore Namibia, mirroring TotalEnergies' Venus discovery dynamics. We're prudently progressing appraisal to de-risk 500 million BOE gross mean resource potential.

Technically, our organic growth stems from several initiatives. We've invested $150 million in advanced geoscience, including machine learning-driven sweet spot mapping and 4D seismic for EOR pilots in the Permian—think CO2 floods targeting 20-30% recovery uplift, akin to Occidental's Oxy Low Carbon Ventures playbook. This has extended our drilling inventory to 8 years at 300,000 BOE/d pace, with 70% Tier 1 locations. We've also reduced cycle times by 25% via pad drilling and simultaneous operations, capitalizing on WTI prices averaging $78 in 2023.

Strategically, this isn't just about replacing reserves—it's about growing them at the low end of the cost curve. Our organic RRR demonstrates capital efficiency: $8.50 per BOE finding and development cost, down from $10.20 in 2022, versus the peer median of $12-15. In a world of energy transition scrutiny, we're balancing this with emissions intensity reductions—down 18% YoY—and scoping studies for CCUS integration. Looking ahead, we expect 2024 organic RRR north of 300%, supported by $2.2 billion capex skewed 75% to Permian development.

These figures are unaudited and subject to year-end SEC review, with sensitivities to commodity prices and regulatory changes. But make no mistake: our reserve book is rock-solid, positioning Apex for shareholder returns through dividends, buybacks, and compounding NAV growth.

Turning to our refining segment, which delivered another strong quarter amid a volatile macro environment. We processed a record 1.25 million barrels per day—up 8% year-over-year and 3% sequentially—while generating segment EBITDA of $850 million, a 15% increase from Q3 2022. This performance was driven by robust throughput, healthy crack spreads, and continued operational excellence across our six U.S.-based refineries, totaling 2.1 million bpd of atmospheric crude distillation capacity.

Our refineries operated at 95% utilization this quarter, the highest in our peer group according to recent S&P Global Platts data, and well above the U.S. Gulf Coast average of 88%. Total throughput averaged 1.25 million bpd, including 1.1 million bpd of crude and 150 thousand bpd of other feedstocks like vacuum gas oil and hydrocracker bottoms from third parties.

Regionally, our Gulf Coast complex—our Beaumont and Port Arthur facilities, with a combined 850 thousand bpd capacity—led the way at 98% utilization, processing 820 thousand bpd. This was fueled by strong availability of advantaged domestic crudes, particularly WTI Midland and Eagle Ford light sours, sourced at $3-5 per barrel discounts to WTI Cushing. Beaumont's coker swallowed 120 thousand bpd of heavy Canadian and Latin American residues, yielding high-value distillates.

On the West Coast, our Los Angeles refinery ran at 92% utilization on 220 thousand bpd, navigating California-specific challenges like elevated renewable diesel blending mandates and logistics constraints from the LA port strikes earlier this year. We opportunistically imported 40 thousand bpd of discounted Oman and Iraqi medium sours via Jones Act waivers. Mid-Continent assets, including our Ponca City and El Dorado plants, hit 94% utilization on 210 thousand bpd, benefiting from local Bakken and Rockies crudes.

Compared to peers like Valero and Marathon Petroleum, our throughput growth outpaced the industry by 500 basis points, thanks to proactive turnaround scheduling—we completed minor planned work at Port Arthur ahead of schedule in Q2, avoiding any Q3 disruptions.

Realized refining margins averaged $18.50 per barrel, up from $14.20 in Q3 2022 and $16.80 in Q2 2023. Our benchmark 3-2-1 crack spread—three barrels of Brent crude to two barrels of Gulf Coast ULSD and one barrel of CBOB RBOB gasoline—averaged $22.10 per barrel Gulf Coast, $24.50 WTI-based, and $20.80 on the West Coast. This reflects sustained distillate strength, with 2:1 diesel cracks hitting $35 per barrel in September amid European refinery outages and IMO 2020-compliant VLSFO demand.

Product slate optimization was key: gasoline yields held at 48% of total output, capturing $0.85/gallon CBOB cracks driven by driving-season demand and summer blendstock needs. Diesel and jet fuel—42% of slate—benefited from a 12% YoY rise in U.S. distillate consumption per EIA data, with jet cracks at $28 per barrel on post-COVID air travel rebound. Our CARB-compliant fuels from LA commanded a $0.15/gallon premium.

Feedstock costs were well-controlled at $78 per barrel net crude cost, 10% below Dated Brent, thanks to our 60/40 light/heavy slate and hedging 50% of Q4 intakes via WTI Midland swaps. RIN costs averaged $1.20 per gallon D4 RINs, flat QoQ, as we banked 15 million excess credits for 2024 compliance under the RFS program. Secondary margins from petrochemicals added $2.10 per barrel, with benzene and toluene yields up 5% via alkylation unit optimizations.

Regionally, Gulf Coast margins were our strongest at $20.50/bbl, outperforming Phillips 66's reported $19.80 due to our higher complexity—average Nelson Complexity Index of 11.2 across the system. West Coast margins at $17.20/bbl faced headwinds from Asian import competition but held firm on premium diesel exports to Mexico.

Efficiency metrics remain industry-leading. Cash operating costs per barrel fell 7% YoY to $5.80, versus Marathon's $6.50 peer average, driven by a 12% reduction in energy intensity to 85 thousand BTUs per barrel—our best ever. This came from deploying digital twin technology at Beaumont, simulating hydrocracker operations to boost middle distillate yields by 2 percentage points to 54%.

Unplanned downtime was just 0.8%—half the U.S. average—thanks to our AI-powered predictive maintenance platform, which flagged 95% of potential failures pre-emptively, avoiding $25 million in lost margin. Turnarounds were flawless: we deferred major work at El Dorado to Q1 2024, saving $50 million in deferrals.

Yield improvements included a 1.5-point lift in total light products to 82% via VGO hydrocracking upgrades at Port Arthur, processing 180 thousand bpd and converting 85% to diesel/jet. We're also ramping renewable diesel co-processing—15 thousand bpd across three units, up 50% YoY—positioning us for 50 thousand bpd nameplate by 2025 under the IRA's 45Z credits, targeting $10/bbl premia.

Variable costs per barrel dropped to $4.20 on lower natural gas prices ($2.50/MMBtu Henry Hub) and our 40% self-generated power from cogeneration. ROCE for the segment hit 28%, top-quartile per Wood Mackenzie benchmarks.

Looking ahead, Q4 throughput guidance is 1.22-1.28 million bpd at 93-97% utilization, with margins of $17-21 per barrel assuming stable cracks. We're advancing our $1.2 billion Beaumont expansion—adding 50 thousand bpd hydrocracker capacity by mid-2025—to capture WTI Midland discounts amid Permian takeaway constraints.

Strategically, we're de-risking via 40% forward hedging on 2024 cracks, blending renewables for D4.5 RINs, and exploring blue hydrogen integration to cut Scope 1 emissions 20% by 2030. In a market with 1.2 million bpd U.S. capacity adds through 2026 but flat demand growth, our complexity and location advantages—proximity to 60% of U.S. crude production—position us to gain share from higher-cost peers like PBF Energy.

Overall, refining underscores our integrated model's resilience.

I will now turn the call over to Michael Rodriguez for an operational update.

Michael Rodriguez: Thank you, Sarah. On the operational front, we continue to execute our strategy effectively. Our production averaged 285,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day. We successfully brought several Delaware Basin wells online, which are expected to contribute significantly to our production growth in the coming quarters. We are also making progress on our cost reduction initiatives.

Good morning, everyone. As we dive into our operational results, I'd like to start with production volumes, which remain the cornerstone of our value creation in this volatile macro environment. At Apex Energy Corp., we're laser-focused on delivering high-margin barrels from our Tier 1 acreage, primarily in the Permian Delaware Basin and the Eagle Ford Shale, while optimizing our Haynesville gas position for downside protection.

Total company-wide production averaged 285,000 BOE/d, marking a robust performance underpinned by our disciplined capital program. Breaking it down: crude oil volumes hit 205,000 barrels per day—that's 72% of our total mix—while natural gas production was 480,000 Mcf/d, equivalent to 80,000 BOE/d after applying our standard 6:1 conversion factor. This oil-heavy profile continues to shield us from Henry Hub weakness, where gas prices averaged just $2.75/MMBtu in the quarter amid oversupply from associated gas flaring cuts in the Permian.

Quarter-over-quarter, from Q2 2024, total production increased 4.5% to 285,000 BOE/d from 272,500 BOE/d. Oil volumes ramped 6% sequentially to 205,000 bbl/d from 193,500 bbl/d, driven primarily by the turn-in-line, or TIL, of 28 new Delaware Basin wells from our Q2 drilling campaign. These Midland-to-Delaware horizontals posted stellar initial production rates averaging 1,800 BOE/d per well, with 65% oil cuts and 30-day IPs exceeding 1,200 bbl/d of oil—right in line with our type curve for the Northern Delaware, where we've now drilled over 150 laterals since acquiring the Waco Heights asset from ConocoPhillips last year.

Gas production dipped 2% QoQ to 480,000 Mcf/d from 490,000 Mcf/d, reflecting base declines in our legacy Eagle Ford dry gas intervals and some voluntary curtailments to preserve reservoir pressure ahead of our planned CO2 flood pilot. Importantly, this sequential oil growth outpaced our Q2 guide by 2,000 BOE/d, thanks to superior execution on frac designs—we've shifted to 4,500-pound proppant per foot with 100-mesh sand and diverter tech, boosting stage-level EURs by 15% per our reservoir models.

Year-over-year, total production surged 18% from Q3 2023's 241,000 BOE/d, with oil volumes leaping 22% to 205,000 bbl/d from 168,000 bbl/d. This YoY lift was fueled by three key drivers: first, the full-quarter impact of our $1.2 billion acquisition of 45,000 net acres in the Permian Black River play from Occidental Petroleum, adding 25,000 BOE/d of high-quality, low-decline production at sub-$40/bbl breakevens; second, accelerated development of our 1,200-location DUC inventory, where we've TIL'd 110 wells year-to-date versus 75 in the prior-year period; and third, enhanced oil recovery initiatives, including waterflood startup in our Eagle Ford Pearsall zone, which arrested declines and added 8,000 bbl/d of incremental oil.

Gas YoY grew a more modest 9% to 480,000 Mcf/d from 440,000 Mcf/d, as we prioritized liquids-rich drilling over Haynesville pure-gas pads amid LNG export ramp-ups straining takeaway capacity. Regionally, our Permian assets—now 65% of total output at 185,000 BOE/d—drove 75% of the YoY growth, with Delaware averaging 120,000 BOE/d (78% oil) versus 95,000 BOE/d last year. Eagle Ford contributed 75,000 BOE/d (55% oil), flat YoY but with improving NGL yields from our upgraded processing at the La Salle plant, while Haynesville gas held steady at 25,000 BOE/d equivalent.

We navigated some headwinds like 3,000 BOE/d of unplanned downtime from third-party power outages in the Permian, reminiscent of the February Texas freeze. We also proactively shut in 10,000 Mcf/d of uneconomic Haynesville gas when prices dipped below $2/MMBtu. Offset by these were tailwinds like WTI averaging $82/bbl, enabling us to high-grade our drilling queue toward 12,000-foot laterals with 50-stage fracs, pushing well costs down to $7.5 million from $8.2 million YoY.

Strategically, these volumes reflect our shift to a 'cash flow machine' model. We're allocating 60% of our $1.1 billion capex to the Permian, targeting 290,000-300,000 BOE/d in Q4 with 72% oil mix, implying 5-7% sequential growth. Longer-term, our PDP inventory supports 3%+ annual organic growth through 2027 at $60 WTI, while EOR pilots could unlock 20-30% EUR uplift on 200 locations. We've hedged 65% of Q4 oil at $78/bbl and 50% gas at $3.10/MMBtu.

In summary, our volumes underscore the resilience of our portfolio. We're not chasing barrels for barrels' sake; every incremental BOE targets sub-$45 breakevens, delivering 50%+ EBITDA margins.

As we continue to deliver strong operational and financial results—our Q3 adjusted EPS came in at $2.45, up 22% year-over-year—I'm pleased to highlight the meaningful progress we're making on our ESG priorities. At Apex Energy, we've embedded sustainability into our core strategy, not just as a compliance exercise, but as a value driver that enhances our license to operate, attracts capital, and positions us competitively in a transitioning energy landscape.

We've set ambitious, science-based targets aligned with the Paris Agreement and the Oil & Gas Climate Initiative (OGCI). Our baseline is 2019, and we're targeting a 40-50% absolute reduction in Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions by 2030, with net-zero Scope 1 and 2 by 2050, excluding non-operated assets and new growth. Scope 3 remains our biggest challenge at over 80% of our footprint, but we're making strides there too through supplier engagement and low-carbon product slates.

Overall GHG intensity: We've reduced our corporate-wide Scope 1 and 2 intensity to 18.2 kg CO2e per BOE, down 12% from Q3 2023 and 28% from our 2019 baseline of 25.3 kg CO2e/BOE. This puts us on track for our 2030 goal of under 15 kg CO2e/BOE, outperforming the 2023 IPIECA industry average of 22 kg CO2e/BOE. Absolute Scope 1 and 2 emissions fell 15% YoY to 4.2 million tCO2e, despite a 5% production uptick to 1.8 million BOE/d, thanks to efficiency gains outpacing volume growth.

Methane intensity dropped to 0.18% of gross gas production, a 22% improvement YoY and 45% below our 2019 baseline of 0.32%. This beats the OGCI target of 0.2% by 2025 and positions us ahead of peers like Chevron's 0.25% and ahead of the EPA's 2024 Permian regulations mandating sub-0.2%. Key drivers include our $250 million investment in continuous monitoring via the Seeking10x initiative—deploying over 2,500 optical gas imaging (OGI) cameras and AI-driven leak detection across our Permian and Bakken assets. We've repaired 1,200+ high-emission sources YTD, capturing 350,000 tCO2e-equivalent, with ROI averaging 3x through avoided fines and gas sales.

Routine flaring intensity is now 0.5% of gross gas, down 35% YoY, aligning with our zero routine flaring by 2028 pledge and World Bank's targets. In the Permian—our largest basin at 45% of production—we've installed 150 vapor recovery units (VRUs) and electrified 60% of our compressor stations, reducing flaring volumes by 40% to under 2 Mcf/BOE.

Regionally: Permian Basin saw 32% YoY Scope 1 reduction to 1.1 MtCO2e, driven by electrification (now 75% of drilling rigs on grid power vs. diesel) and CCUS pilots. Our Glass Mountain CCUS hub, in partnership with Occidental, is capturing 500 ktCO2/year from nearby steamflood ops, with Phase 2 FID expected Q4.

North Sea (Norway/UK): Intensity at 12 kg CO2e/BOE, 20% below the 2023 Norwegian Petroleum Directorate average. Full electrification of our Troll field platforms by 2026 will cut emissions 50%, leveraging Norway's hydropower grid—similar to Equinor's approach.

Middle East/Guyana (non-op): Scope 1 emissions down 18% via JV-led initiatives like ADNOC's mangrove restoration offsetting 100 ktCO2e. In Guyana, our Stabroek block partners (Exxon-led) hit 95% flare gas capture.

We've accelerated high-impact programs: Electrification Roadmap with $1.2 billion committed through 2027, targeting 90% of upstream power from renewables/low-carbon sources, including PPAs for 500 MW solar/wind in Texas and microgrids in Bakken. CCUS Expansion: Beyond Glass Mountain, our Alberta hub is at 1 MtCO2/year capacity, with 45Q tax credits enhancing economics—internal rate of return >15% at $50/tonne CO2. Digital Twins and AI rolled out across 80% of facilities, predicting 95% of leaks preemptively. Hydrogen Blending: Piloting 20% blue hydrogen in gas plants, reducing CO2 by 40%—scalable to LNG cargoes.

These deliver $180 million in annual savings from energy efficiency and methane capture, plus a 15% lower cost of capital via ESG-linked bonds. Looking ahead, with Brent at $82/bbl and WTI $78, we're funding this through free cash flow—no dilution. Regulatory tailwinds like IRA incentives and EU CBAM are pushing us, but so is investor demand—our ESG score jumped to A from BB by Sustainalytics. Q4 guidance holds emissions intensity flat-to-down QoQ, with full-year on track for 25% reduction from baseline. This disciplined approach de-risks our 10% CAGR production growth to 2 MMBOE/d by 2028 while advancing energy transition leadership.

Now I will turn it over to Lisa Chen for an update on our exploration activities.

Lisa Chen: Thank you, Michael. We are excited about the potential of our exploration program. We recently completed a successful seismic survey in the Permian Basin and are planning to drill 20 exploration wells in the next year. We believe these wells have the potential to add significant reserves to our portfolio, building on our strong organic reserve replacement and regional successes in Delaware, Eagle Ford, Bakken, and offshore assets.

Operator, we are now ready to open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Brian Scott with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Brian Scott: Good morning. Can you provide more detail on your debt reduction strategy and leverage outlook?

David Thompson: Good morning, Brian. As Sarah detailed, we've made excellent progress deleveraging through free cash flow from high-margin operations, with total debt down 8% to $12.4 billion and net debt at $9.8 billion, achieving 1.2x leverage. We're on track for sub-$9 billion net debt by year-end, supported by asset sales and hedging, while maintaining flexibility for returns and growth.

Operator: Our next question comes from Emily Chen with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Emily Chen: Good morning. What are your expectations for refining margins and throughput in Q4?

Sarah Jenkins: Good morning, Emily. We're guiding 1.22-1.28 million bpd throughput at 93-97% utilization, with $17-21 per barrel margins assuming stable cracks. Our high-complexity assets and feedstock advantages position us well to capture upside from distillate demand and Permian discounts.

Operator: Our next question comes from Robert Kline with Citigroup. Please go ahead.

Robert Kline: Could you please provide more color on production volumes outlook and regional drivers?

Michael Rodriguez: Thanks, Robert. We're targeting 290,000-300,000 BOE/d in Q4, with Permian leading at 65% of output and continued oil growth from Delaware TILs and EOR. YoY gains from acquisitions and efficiencies keep us at high-margin breakevens.

Operator: Our next question comes from Laura Patel with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Laura Patel: How will the results of the exploration program affect the company's future strategy?

Lisa Chen: Great question, Laura. Our Permian seismic and 20 planned wells build on 380% organic RRR, extending inventory with Tier 1 locations. Successes here will skew capex toward development, enhancing reserves and supporting 3%+ organic growth while integrating with CCUS for ESG alignment.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I would like to turn the conference back over to David Thompson for closing remarks.

David Thompson: Thank you, Operator. In summary, we are pleased with our performance in Q3. We remain focused on executing our strategy and delivering value to our shareholders. Thank you for joining us today.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
